issue_context.title: Harden default ESP/XBOOTLDR automount
issue_context.body:
### Component

systemd-gpt-auto-generator

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe

`boot.mount` (as created by automounting) can potentially be hardened further without affecting the majority of setups (at least as far as I know, please say if not).

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add `noexec` and maybe `nosuid` to the `Options` line in `boot.mount` by default. The thinking being:

- `noexec`: There's no reason for anything executable by the OS to be in here.
- `nodev`: Automounts don't create nested mounts to `/boot/efi`, so mounting a device under `/boot` won't be needed. But, future loopback devices won't work.
- `nosuid`: Not sure if FAT32 can even handle `suid` bits, so this one's unclear.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

If some of these options do conflict with a significant number of setups, or aren't as useful if FAT32 lacks the capability anyways, only adding some of these options would be fine (but to be honest, I'd be fine with none getting through if it turns out all of them are each too restrictive; this issue would be useful as reference).

### The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for

252.3-1-arch
comments:
> * `noexec`: There's no reason for anything executable by the OS to be in here.

Why restrict people to place special purpose scripts/binaries in `/boot` at all by default?
The files in `/boot` include (by purpose) files **to-be executed**, although mostly by the BIOS/UEFI instead of the Kernel, but you can imagine people wanting to place utilities there...
fe. to generate PK/MoK keys that is shared between multiple OS's, to keep them in one spot.
_(Ofcourse these being on a USB etc)_

> * `nodev`: Automounts don't create nested mounts to `/boot/efi`, so mounting a device under `/boot` won't be needed. But, future loopback devices won't work.

It's rather normal practice to mount the `$ESP` on `/boot/efi` after `/boot` is mounted.
I even "bind-mount" `$ESP/xxxx` as `/boot` or `$ESP` as `/boot/efi` when/as needed :wink: 

PS: Isn't `nodev` related to something different as a mount-point, like `/dev/sda`?

> * `nosuid`: Not sure if FAT32 can even handle `suid` bits, so this one's unclear.

By the way the `/boot` partition can (IIRC) also be another filesystem type beside FAT32.
Think about grub that supports `btrfs` as example, or `ntfs` etc...
_(In the case of grub, the `noexec` above would even interfere i think)_

You are probably mistaking the `/boot` partition with the `$ESP`, which doesn't have to be the same...

---
So to conclude from my side: No thanks for these :vulcan_salute:

@TriMoon You're right, I just realised `boot.mount` literally means whatever is mounted at `/boot`, and not the ESP or XBOOTLDR specifically. In that case, the following is probably better(?):

For `efi.mount`:
- `noexec` is likely off the table due to boot scripts.
- `nodev` is fine for `efi.mount` since it won't prevent `/boot/efi`.
- `nosuid` is still unclear, `/efi` is always the ESP which (nearly always) must be FAT32, but I'm not sure adding this option prevents anything.

For `boot.mount` (XBOOTLDR only):

- `noexec` is likely off the table due to boot scripts.
- `nodev` might be fine assuming https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/3757#issuecomment-234278327 is true and automount never creates `/boot/efi` mounts (although the bind-mount case wouldn't work as you said).
- `nosuid` can protect XBOOTLDR if it's a non-FAT filesystem, which it can be.
Is it possible for systemd to change `boot.mount`'s default options depending on if the ESP or XBOOTLDR is being used?
On second thoughts, yeah, this isn't a good idea; there's too many options when talking about boot scripts to even use `nosuid` without affecting at least something. Closing issue

Actualy I think we should probably enable these mount options if gpt-auto-discovery mounts these file systems. 

ESP and XBOOTLDR have pretty clear purposes (resources for the boot loader).

Distros which don't make use of the gpt-auto-discovery and create a manual mount entry for the ESP in /boot/efi/ can pick their own options after all, and are not affected by what gpt-auto-discovery does.

Distros mounting the ESP to /boot/efi/ is pretty stupid btw, people shouldn#t nest that, distros should stop that nonsense.

@poettering , just a side-question: Wondering about `gpt-auto-discovery`...

Does `gpt-auto-discovery` count for multiple `$ESP`'s on different disks?
I know that `sd-boot` provides the used `$ESP` to the OS, but how about other boot loaders?

In case non of the bootloaders used, provide the actual used `$ESP` to the OS:
- How does `gpt-auto-discovery` decide which one to mount as `$ESP` ?

---
> Distros mounting the ESP to /boot/efi/ is pretty stupid btw, people shouldn#t nest that, distros should stop that nonsense.

I couldn't agree more :rofl:

> @poettering , just a side-question: Wondering about `gpt-auto-discovery`...
> 
> Does `gpt-auto-discovery` count for multiple `$ESP`'s on different disks?

No. It only mounts the ESP on the disk backing the root fs, and only if it was the one the firmware actually used for booting.

gpt-auto-discovery is actually two things:

1. mount the rootfs is root= is not specified on kernel cmdline. here we look for the root fs exclusively on the disk the ESP used for booting is on.
2. mount all other related partitions. Here we look for the partitions on the same disk as the root fs used.

These two parts are fairly independent. For the first item to work we need a boot loader that tells userspace the used ESP. For the second part we don't however.

anyway, no raid in any of this.
